chunks.text: Hamstring strain injuries: recommendations for diagnosis, rehabilitation, and injury prevention. Hamstring strain injuries: recommendations for diagnosis, rehabilitation, and injury prevention. Hamstring strain injuries are common in sports involving high-speed running and are prone to recurrence.

Hamstring strain injuries are common in sports involving high-speed running and are prone to recurrence. Two principal mechanisms are described: high-speed running injuries, typically affecting the biceps femoris long head at the proximal musculotendinous junction during the late swing phase of gait where the muscle contracts eccentrically to decelerate the swinging tibia; and stretch-type injuries from combined hip flexion and knee extension, more often involving the proximal free tendon of semimembranosus and taking longer to recover.

Two principal mechanisms are described: high-speed running injuries, typically affecting the biceps femoris long head at the proximal musculotendinous junction during the late swing phase of gait where the muscle contracts eccentrically to decelerate the swinging tibia; and stretch-type injuries from combined hip flexion and knee extension, more often involving the proximal free tendon of semimembranosus and taking longer to recover. Diagnosis includes location of maximal tenderness, its distance from the ischial tuberosity, and the extent of pain-free range.

Diagnosis includes location of maximal tenderness, its distance from the ischial tuberosity, and the extent of pain-free range. Rehabilitation should progress based on clinical criteria rather than time alone, emphasising neuromuscular control of the lumbopelvic region, eccentric strengthening of the hamstrings at longer muscle lengths, and progressive agility and trunk stabilisation. Return-to-sport criteria include full strength and pain-free maximal effort.

Return-to-sport criteria include full strength and pain-free maximal effort. Injuries involving the intramuscular (central) tendon and greater cross-sectional or longitudinal extent of injury are associated with longer recovery.

A comparison of 2 rehabilitation programs in the treatment of acute hamstring strains. A comparison of 2 rehabilitation programs in the treatment of acute hamstring strains. Randomised comparison of two rehabilitation programmes for acute hamstring strain. A programme of progressive agility and trunk stabilisation (PATS) was compared with a programme of static stretching and isolated hamstring strengthening (STST).

A programme of progressive agility and trunk stabilisation (PATS) was compared with a programme of static stretching and isolated hamstring strengthening (STST). Although time to return to sport was similar between groups, the reinjury rate within the first two weeks and within one year of return to sport was substantially lower in the progressive agility and trunk stabilisation group.

Although time to return to sport was similar between groups, the reinjury rate within the first two weeks and within one year of return to sport was substantially lower in the progressive agility and trunk stabilisation group. The findings suggest that isolated hamstring stretching and strengthening is inferior to a programme emphasising neuromuscular control of the pelvis and trunk together with movement-based progression, and that reinjury — not return time — is the key outcome distinguishing rehabilitation quality.

Acute hamstring injuries in Swedish elite football: a prospective randomised controlled clinical trial comparing two rehabilitation protocols. Acute hamstring injuries in Swedish elite football: a prospective randomised controlled clinical trial comparing two rehabilitation protocols.

Acute hamstring injuries in Swedish elite football: a prospective randomised controlled clinical trial comparing two rehabilitation protocols. Randomised controlled trial in elite footballers comparing a rehabilitation protocol emphasising lengthening (eccentric) exercises performed at longer muscle lengths (the L-protocol, three exercises: the 'extender', 'diver', and 'glider') against a conventional protocol of concentric and isometric exercises (the C-protocol).

Randomised controlled trial in elite footballers comparing a rehabilitation protocol emphasising lengthening (eccentric) exercises performed at longer muscle lengths (the L-protocol, three exercises: the 'extender', 'diver', and 'glider') against a conventional protocol of concentric and isometric exercises (the C-protocol). The lengthening protocol produced significantly shorter time to return to play (mean around 28 days versus 51 days).

The lengthening protocol produced significantly shorter time to return to play (mean around 28 days versus 51 days). The trial supports early introduction of controlled lengthening loads that stress the hamstring near its end-range, rather than avoiding lengthening, and highlights the importance of loading the muscle at the lengths at which running injuries occur.

Acute hamstring injuries in Swedish elite sprinters and jumpers: a prospective randomised controlled clinical trial comparing two rehabilitation protocols. Acute hamstring injuries in Swedish elite sprinters and jumpers: a prospective randomised controlled clinical trial comparing two rehabilitation protocols. Randomised controlled trial in elite sprinters and jumpers comparing the lengthening (L) protocol with a conventional (C) protocol for acute hamstring injury.

Randomised controlled trial in elite sprinters and jumpers comparing the lengthening (L) protocol with a conventional (C) protocol for acute hamstring injury. As in the football cohort, the lengthening protocol emphasising exercises at long muscle lengths resulted in markedly shorter time to return to sport.

As in the football cohort, the lengthening protocol emphasising exercises at long muscle lengths resulted in markedly shorter time to return to sport. The consistency of the effect across sprint/jump and football athletes strengthens the case for lengthening-biased loading as a core rehabilitation principle for hamstring strain, provided loads are introduced progressively and remain within a tolerable symptom range.

British athletics muscle injury classification: a new grading system. British athletics muscle injury classification: a new grading system. The British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC) grades muscle injuries 0 to 4 by MRI extent and adds a site suffix indicating the anatomical location of injury: 'a' myofascial (peripheral), 'b' musculotendinous, and 'c' intratendinous (involving the tendon itself).

The British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC) grades muscle injuries 0 to 4 by MRI extent and adds a site suffix indicating the anatomical location of injury: 'a' myofascial (peripheral), 'b' musculotendinous, and 'c' intratendinous (involving the tendon itself). The classification was developed to improve prognostication over older grade 1/2/3 systems.

The classification was developed to improve prognostication over older grade 1/2/3 systems. Injuries involving the intramuscular tendon (c-grade) carry a worse prognosis and higher reinjury risk, and typically require a more conservative and prolonged rehabilitation. The system links imaging findings to expected recovery time and informs return-to-play decision-making.

The preventive effect of the Nordic hamstring exercise on hamstring injuries in amateur soccer players: a randomized controlled trial. The preventive effect of the Nordic hamstring exercise on hamstring injuries in amateur soccer players: a randomized controlled trial. Cluster randomised controlled trial in amateur soccer players evaluating a 13-week Nordic hamstring exercise programme for prevention of hamstring injuries.

Cluster randomised controlled trial in amateur soccer players evaluating a 13-week Nordic hamstring exercise programme for prevention of hamstring injuries. The intervention group performed a structured, progressive Nordic hamstring programme in addition to regular training; the control group trained as usual. The incidence of acute hamstring injuries was significantly reduced in the Nordic group.

The incidence of acute hamstring injuries was significantly reduced in the Nordic group. The study reinforces eccentric strengthening via the Nordic hamstring exercise as an effective primary-prevention measure, and supports its inclusion in late-stage rehabilitation and return-to-sport conditioning to reduce reinjury risk.

Preventive effect of eccentric training on acute hamstring injuries in men's soccer: a cluster-randomized controlled trial. Preventive effect of eccentric training on acute hamstring injuries in men's soccer: a cluster-randomized controlled trial. Cluster-randomised controlled trial of 942 male soccer players evaluating a 10-week progressive Nordic hamstring exercise programme.

Cluster-randomised controlled trial of 942 male soccer players evaluating a 10-week progressive Nordic hamstring exercise programme. Eccentric training substantially reduced the rate of new and recurrent acute hamstring injuries compared with controls, with a particularly strong protective effect against recurrent injuries.

Eccentric training substantially reduced the rate of new and recurrent acute hamstring injuries compared with controls, with a particularly strong protective effect against recurrent injuries. The study provides high-quality evidence that eccentric hamstring strengthening reduces both first-time and recurrent hamstring strains, and is a cornerstone of the evidence base for including Nordic-type eccentric loading in prevention and end-stage rehabilitation.

Pain-free versus pain-threshold rehabilitation following acute hamstring strain injury: a randomized controlled trial. Pain-free versus pain-threshold rehabilitation following acute hamstring strain injury: a randomized controlled trial. Randomised controlled trial comparing pain-free versus pain-threshold rehabilitation after acute hamstring strain injury.

Randomised controlled trial comparing pain-free versus pain-threshold rehabilitation after acute hamstring strain injury. In the pain-threshold group, patients were permitted to work into a tolerable level of pain during exercises; the pain-free group avoided any pain. Time to return to sport was similar between groups, and there were no significant differences in reinjury rates.

Time to return to sport was similar between groups, and there were no significant differences in reinjury rates. Allowing exercise into a tolerable, controlled level of pain did not compromise outcomes, suggesting rehabilitation loading need not be strictly pain-free and can progress based on tolerable symptom response rather than complete absence of pain.

A multifactorial, criteria-based progressive algorithm for hamstring injury treatment. A multifactorial, criteria-based progressive algorithm for hamstring injury treatment. Presents a multifactorial, criteria-based progressive algorithm for hamstring injury rehabilitation that advances athletes through phases according to objective clinical criteria rather than fixed timelines.

Presents a multifactorial, criteria-based progressive algorithm for hamstring injury rehabilitation that advances athletes through phases according to objective clinical criteria rather than fixed timelines. Domains monitored include pain, range of motion, strength (including eccentric and at long muscle lengths), lumbopelvic control, and progressive running and sprint exposure.

Domains monitored include pain, range of motion, strength (including eccentric and at long muscle lengths), lumbopelvic control, and progressive running and sprint exposure. Progression from one phase to the next requires meeting criteria within each domain, and return to sport requires restoration of strength symmetry, completion of a graded high-speed running and sprinting programme, and demonstration of sport-specific capacity.

Progression from one phase to the next requires meeting criteria within each domain, and return to sport requires restoration of strength symmetry, completion of a graded high-speed running and sprinting programme, and demonstration of sport-specific capacity. The framework operationalises individualised, criteria-driven decision-making and is designed to reduce reinjury by ensuring athletes are exposed to maximal sprinting loads before clearance.

Epidemiology of muscle injuries in professional football (soccer). Epidemiology of muscle injuries in professional football (soccer). Prospective cohort of professional football teams over multiple seasons quantifying muscle injury burden. Muscle injuries accounted for approximately one third of all time-loss injuries, and the hamstrings were the most commonly injured muscle group, representing a large share of the total.

Muscle injuries accounted for approximately one third of all time-loss injuries, and the hamstrings were the most commonly injured muscle group, representing a large share of the total. A substantial proportion of hamstring injuries were recurrences, and reinjuries caused longer absences than index injuries. The data establish hamstring strain as the single most burdensome injury in football and underline reinjury prevention as the central clinical priority.

At return to play following hamstring injury the majority of professional football players have residual isokinetic deficits. At return to play following hamstring injury the majority of professional football players have residual isokinetic deficits. Prospective study of professional footballers cleared to return to play after hamstring injury by usual clinical criteria.

Prospective study of professional footballers cleared to return to play after hamstring injury by usual clinical criteria. Despite clinical clearance, the majority still had measurable isokinetic strength deficits in the previously injured limb at the time of return.

Despite clinical clearance, the majority still had measurable isokinetic strength deficits in the previously injured limb at the time of return. The finding demonstrates that symptom resolution and clinical examination alone are insufficient to confirm restored capacity, and argues for objective strength testing (including eccentric and limb-symmetry measures) as part of return-to-sport decision-making to reduce reinjury risk.

Intramuscular platelet-rich plasma injection in acute hamstring injury: a randomized controlled trial. Intramuscular platelet-rich plasma injection in acute hamstring injury: a randomized controlled trial. Randomised controlled trial evaluating a single intramuscular platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection versus placebo (or no injection) in addition to a standardised rehabilitation programme for acute hamstring injury.

Randomised controlled trial evaluating a single intramuscular platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection versus placebo (or no injection) in addition to a standardised rehabilitation programme for acute hamstring injury. There was no significant difference between groups in time to return to sport or in reinjury rate.

There was no significant difference between groups in time to return to sport or in reinjury rate. The trial provides evidence that PRP injection does not improve outcomes over an exercise-based rehabilitation programme for acute hamstring strain, reinforcing progressive loading rehabilitation — rather than biological injection — as the effective intervention.

An evidence-based framework for strengthening exercises to prevent hamstring injury. An evidence-based framework for strengthening exercises to prevent hamstring injury. Systematic review synthesising the evidence for strengthening exercises to prevent hamstring injury.

Systematic review synthesising the evidence for strengthening exercises to prevent hamstring injury. Eccentric exercises that load the hamstrings at longer muscle lengths — most notably the Nordic hamstring exercise — increase biceps femoris fascicle length and eccentric strength, both of which are associated with reduced injury risk.

Eccentric exercises that load the hamstrings at longer muscle lengths — most notably the Nordic hamstring exercise — increase biceps femoris fascicle length and eccentric strength, both of which are associated with reduced injury risk. The review frames exercise selection by the biomechanical demands they impose (hip-extension versus knee-flexion bias, and the muscle length at which peak load occurs) and recommends combining exercises to cover the spectrum of demands, providing a rationale for exercise selection in both prevention and late-stage rehabilitation.

Reinjury after acute posterior thigh muscle injuries in elite track and field athletes. Reinjury after acute posterior thigh muscle injuries in elite track and field athletes. Prospective study of acute posterior thigh (hamstring) muscle injuries in elite track and field athletes examining reinjury. A meaningful proportion of athletes sustained a reinjury, most within the early period after return.

A meaningful proportion of athletes sustained a reinjury, most within the early period after return. Delayed recovery of pain-free range of motion and inadequate rehabilitation progression were associated with reinjury. The study supports restoration of full pain-free flexibility and criteria-based progression before return, and identifies the early post-return window as the period of highest reinjury vulnerability.
